text: The three-second goldfish memory is a myth. Goldfish have learned to press a lever for food when it worked only one hour a day, and fish trained to tell odors apart still remembered them three months later.

The tongue map, with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back, is wrong. It grew from a 1901 German study that found only slight differences in sensitivity; every region with taste buds detects every basic taste.
The claim that bacteria outnumber your cells ten to one traces to a rough 1972 estimate. A 2016 recount found about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells, roughly one to one.
Radiocarbon in the eye lenses of Greenland sharks suggests the largest one studied was about 392 years old, give or take about 120 years, making it the longest-lived vertebrate known.
The largest genome measured belongs to Tmesipteris oblanceolata, a small fern from New Caledonia: about 160 billion base pairs, some 50 times the human genome. Nobody knows why it carries so much.
The often-quoted 100 billion neurons in the human brain was never actually counted. In 2009 researchers dissolved brains into a countable suspension of cell nuclei and found about 86 billion.
In 2010 the first cell with a fully synthetic genome carried quotations coded into its DNA. One misquoted Richard Feynman, whose blackboard read "What I cannot create, I do not understand."
The minimal synthetic cell JCVI-syn3.0 (2016) lives on just 473 genes, yet 149 of them had no known function. Even the simplest life we can build is not fully understood.
Peto's paradox: an elephant has vastly more cells than a mouse, so it should get far more cancer, yet it does not. Elephants carry about 20 copies of the tumor-suppressor gene TP53; humans have one.
Mantis shrimp have 12 types of color receptor to our three, yet in tests they told colors apart worse than humans do. They seem to recognize colors quickly rather than compare them finely.
When measles struck the isolated Faroe Islands in 1846, the physician Peter Panum noticed that old people who had caught it in the previous outbreak, in 1781, were still immune 65 years later.
Lynn Margulis's 1967 paper arguing that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria was rejected by about 15 journals before it was published. The idea is now textbook science.
Cancer is not just a modern disease. A hominin foot bone about 1.7 million years old, from Swartkrans Cave in South Africa, shows osteosarcoma, an aggressive bone cancer.

In 1862 Darwin predicted that a Madagascar orchid with a very long nectar spur needed a moth with an equally long tongue. The moth, described in 1903, was named praedicta for Wallace's 1867 prediction, not Darwin's.
By mass, wild mammals are now only about 4% of Earth's mammals. Livestock make up roughly 60% and humans about 36%, according to a 2018 census of the biosphere.

Upside-down jellyfish have no brain, yet in 2017 researchers found they sleep: they pulse less at night, respond slowly, and catch up after being kept awake. Why sleep evolved is still an open question.
No one has ever seen European eels spawn or found their eggs in the wild. Larval surveys point to the Sargasso Sea, and in 2022 satellite tags tracked adults arriving there for the first time.

"The Creator would appear as endowed with a passion for stars, on the one hand, and for beetles on the other." (J. B. S. Haldane, What Is Life?, 1949) The "inordinate fondness" version is a later retelling.
"Nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution." (Theodosius Dobzhansky, essay in The American Biology Teacher, 1973)
"From so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved." (Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859)
Lemmings do not commit mass suicide. The cliff scene in Disney's 1958 film White Wilderness was staged, with the animals driven over the edge by the filmmakers; the fakery was exposed in 1982.
In 1984 Barry Marshall drank a broth of Helicobacter pylori to show that bacteria inflame the stomach. He developed gastritis, and he and Robin Warren later shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.
Mimivirus, found in 1992 in a cooling tower in Bradford, England, is so large that it was first mistaken for a bacterium. Only in 2003 was it recognized as a virus.
About 8% of the human genome is the remains of ancient retroviruses. One of their genes, now called syncytin, helps fuse cells into the placenta's outer layer: pregnancy relies on a tamed virus.
In 1898 Thomas Hunt Morgan found that a piece of planarian flatworm about 1/279 of its body could regrow into a whole worm. Stem cells called neoblasts make this possible.
CC, the first cloned cat (2001), did not look like her calico donor. Calico patches depend on which X chromosome each early cell randomly switches off, and that pattern is not copied by cloning.
People conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944 to 1945 still showed lower DNA methylation of the IGF2 gene six decades later than their unexposed siblings.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings. Researchers traced the shape to stiffer and stretchier bands in the intestine wall, work that won a 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in physics.
Pando, a grove of about 47,000 quaking aspen trunks in Utah, is a single clone sharing one root system. At an estimated 6,000 metric tons, it may be the heaviest living organism.
Hair and nails do not keep growing after death. As the body dries, the skin retracts and exposes more of each nail and hair shaft, which creates the illusion.
